# Browser tests with Geb

Still `@Integration`, just from the outside with a real browser

<!--
⏱ 19:45 — Browser tests, about seven minutes.

As we saw in the landscape: a Geb spec is an integration spec with a browser attached. What this section adds is the browser, and, optionally, a phase of your own to run it in.
-->

---

# What changed in Grails 7

<div class="grid grid-cols-2 gap-10 text-[0.9em]">
<div>

### Before: a browser on every machine

```groovy
// build.gradle, generated by Grails 6.0.0
plugins {
    id 'com.github.erdi.webdriver-binaries' version '3.0'
}
webdriverBinaries {
    chromedriver '110.0.5481.77'
    geckodriver '0.32.2'
}
```

- Chrome updates itself, the pinned driver doesn’t
- Every laptop and CI image needs the right browser installed
- A `GebConfig.groovy` driver per browser, picked with `-Dgeb.env`

</div>
<div>

### Now: the browser in a container

<v-clicks>

- `ContainerGebSpec`: same Geb API, browser in a **Testcontainers** Selenium container
- The image follows your Selenium version: browser and driver always match
- Only Docker needed, the same browser everywhere
- Since Dec 2024: Grails 6 (Geb plugin 4.1) and 7, the Forge default
- `GebSpec` still works, with the browsers on your machine
- Now in Apache Geb as `geb-testcontainers`, not released yet

</v-clicks>

</div>
</div>

<!--
Before Grails 7, browser tests drove a browser installed on your machine. This is what a Grails 6 app generated for them.

The webdriver-binaries plugin downloaded a ChromeDriver pinned in your build, version 110 here. Chrome updates itself every few weeks; the pinned driver doesn’t. So one day the browser tests fail with a version mismatch, on one laptop and not the other.

On CI the build used whatever drivers the runner image happened to have. And every machine needed the browsers installed.

[click] So in October 2024 we added ContainerGebSpec to the Grails Geb plugin. Same Geb API, but the browser runs in a Selenium container that Testcontainers manages.

[click] The image tag matches the Selenium version on your classpath, so the driver and the browser always belong together.

[click] All a machine needs is a container runtime. The same browser runs on every laptop and on CI.

[click] It was first released in December 2024, in the Geb plugin 4.1 for Grails 6. Others added recording and reporting soon after, and in Grails 7 a new app from Forge comes with a ContainerGebSpec by default.

[click] And GebSpec hasn’t gone anywhere. If you’d rather use the browsers on your machine, pick geb-with-local-browsers in Forge: a plain GebSpec, one GebConfig environment per browser, and Selenium Manager fetches the matching driver.

[click] And the upstream Apache Geb project has added a geb-testcontainers module, derived from the Grails module, so any web app can use it. It isn’t released yet.
-->

# `GebSpec` → `ContainerGebSpec`

````md magic-move {lines: false}
```groovy
import geb.spock.GebSpec
import grails.testing.mixin.integration.Integration

@Integration
class HomeSpec extends GebSpec {

    void 'home page renders'() {
        when:
            go('/')

        then:
            waitFor { title == 'Welcome to Grails' }
    }
}
```

```groovy
import grails.plugin.geb.ContainerGebSpec
import grails.testing.mixin.integration.Integration

@Integration
class HomeSpec extends ContainerGebSpec {

    void 'home page renders'() {
        when:
            go('/')

        then:
            waitFor { title == 'Welcome to Grails' }
    }
}
```
````

<!--
Here is a classic GebSpec, the way a Grails 6 app would have it.

[click] To migrate, change the import and the base class. The Geb API you use in the body is identical. For a spec like this, that is the whole migration.
-->

---

# What `ContainerGebSpec` brings

<div class="grid grid-cols-2 gap-8 small feature-grid">
<div>

### Recording & reporting

```groovy
tasks.named('integrationTest') {
    systemProperty('grails.geb.recording.mode', 'RECORD_FAILING')
}
```

`SKIP` · `RECORD_ALL` · `RECORD_FAILING` → `build/gebContainer/recordings/*.mp4`

`@ContainerGebConfiguration(reporting = true)` → screenshots & page source in `build/gebContainer/reports`

### Host & context path

```groovy
@ContainerGebConfiguration(hostName = 'testing.example.com')
```

`server.servlet.context-path` is picked up automatically

</div>
<div>

### Timeouts & waiting

System properties instead of `GebConfig.groovy` edits: `grails.geb.timeouts.timeout`, `retryInterval`, `pageLoad`, `implicitlyWait`, `grails.geb.atCheckWaiting.enabled`

### Uploads

`uploadFile('/tmp/data.csv')` copies the file into the browser container first

### Your own driver

A `GebConfig.groovy` on the test classpath still wins: Firefox, another Selenium image, your own `RemoteWebDriver`

</div>
</div>

<style>
.feature-grid h3 { font-size: 1.05em; margin: 0.5em 0 0.15em; color: var(--grails-orange); }
.feature-grid p { margin: 0.25em 0; line-height: 1.35; }
</style>

<!--
⏱ 23:00

A tour of the extras, because the base class is more than a driver factory.

Recording: one system property and every test, or every failing test, becomes an MP4 in the build directory. Reporting gives you Geb’s screenshots and page source on failure. Both are wonderful on CI.

Host name matters when your app cares about the Host header. Context path is picked up automatically since 7.1.

Timeouts and waiting are configurable with system properties rather than editing GebConfig.

Uploads work: the file is automatically copied into the container before the browser selects it.

And if you need a different browser or image, a GebConfig.groovy still takes precedence.
-->

<!--
⏱ 24:15

Here is a complete browser spec. It lives in its own functionalTest phase, which we’ll declare in a minute, but nothing in the class knows that: put it in src/integration-test and it runs the same.

It’s a ContainerGebSpec with @Integration.

[click] `to(HomePage)` navigates to a Geb page object and returns it. Assigning it to a variable is what gives you IDE completion on the page content,

[click] and `heading` is content defined on that page.

[click] As a side note: since this is an ordinary @Integration test, running in the same JVM as the app, we can also work with the app directly, not just through the browser. Here the test data is created straight through GORM, in a new transaction so it is committed and visible to the browser.

[click] Then the assertion reads against page content again, `people` on a PeoplePage this time, which wraps the jQuery-like selector `$('ul#people li')`.

# Simulated latency <span class="badge">new in 8.0</span>

<div class="grid grid-cols-2 gap-10">
<div>

```groovy
// build.gradle
dependencies {
    functionalTestRuntimeOnly '…:grails-testing-support-latency'
}
tasks.named('functionalTest') {
    if (project.hasProperty('latency')) {
        systemProperty('grails.testing.latency.enabled', 'true')
    }
}
```

```yaml
# application.yml, test environment
grails.testing.latency:
    min-delay: 250ms
    max-delay: 2s          # the default
    probability: 0.5       # delay half the requests
    url-patterns: /api/*   # default /*
    seed: 42               # reproducible sequence
```

</div>
<div>

A servlet filter, first in the chain, sleeps a random time before each matching request.

```text
./gradlew functionalTest -Platency

Delaying GET / by 1559ms
Delaying GET /assets/…/bootstrap.css by 1495ms
Delaying GET /assets/grails.svg by 1866ms
…  34 requests delayed, both specs still green
```

<v-clicks>

- A test that races a click-triggered navigation now **fails every time**, not now and then on CI
- **Never enable it in production config**

</v-clicks>

</div>
</div>

<!--
⏱ 25:45

Simulated latency, new in Grails 8: its job is to flush out flaky browser tests. A missing waitFor, or an assertion that reads the page before it has loaded, never shows on your laptop, where the server answers in milliseconds. On a busy CI runner it fails now and then.

This module makes the server slow on purpose. It does nothing until you enable it, here with a Gradle property. You set the minimum and maximum delay, how many requests to slow down, which URLs, and a seed to repeat the same delays.

On the right is a real run: every request waited up to two seconds, and the specs still passed, because Geb waits for pages to load.

[click] A test that races the server now fails every time, so you can fix it.

[click] And of course, only in tests, never in production.
-->
